title: Decision Models and Generalised Classifiers
subtitle: From BERT-style classifiers to the new System One decision models: typed questions, calibration, evaluation and routing, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on introduction to generalised classifiers and the new category of decision models, also called System One models. Learn how classifiers, encoders and ModernBERT work; zero-shot and embedding classification; the typed-question interface of boolean, choice and score answers; the masked-option encoder design reported for Laya; the prefill-only decoder design reported for Clef, with joint and pointer heads and KV-cache reuse; calibration with temperature scaling, ECE, Brier score and log loss; evaluation on your own data; and routing, cascades, guardrails and escalation in real systems. The field is only weeks old, so vendor figures are marked as reported and the course stresses durable concepts. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus a decision playground and a calibration lab.

chapters.title: From classifiers to decision models

maps.title: Decision models
links: Decision model | answers | A typed question
System one | is | Fast and one pass
Router | picks | Cheap or costly path

summary: A classifier reads input and picks a label. A decision model is the newer idea of a small model that answers a typed question about some input, such as yes or no, one of these options, or a score from 0 to 1, in a single forward pass and with calibrated probabilities.

The pitch is a split of labour. Fast System One models make the many routine decisions cheaply, and slow System Two models, the large reasoning LLMs, handle what is hard or uncertain. The idea is new, so products and numbers change quickly and vendor claims need checking.
This course starts with the durable concepts: encoders, calibration, evaluation and routing. Vendor details are marked as reported as of late 2026.

glossary.def: A model mapping an input to one of a fixed set of labels.
A compact model that answers a typed question about an input in one pass and returns a calibrated probability or score.
Fast, automatic judgement, borrowed from psychology to describe one-pass models.
Slow, deliberate reasoning, here meaning large reasoning models that think step by step.
Agreement between stated confidence and how often the answer is right.

keyPoints: One forward pass, no chain of thought.
Route easy cases here, hard cases to an LLM.
Treat vendor numbers as claims to verify.

items: ELI5. A quick helper at the front desk can point visitors to the right room in a second. Only the odd questions go to the busy expert upstairs.

Many software decisions are small. Is this message spam? Is this ticket about billing or shipping? Does this answer follow the policy? Which of five tools should the agent call? Asking a large language model each time works, but it is slow, costs money, and its text answers must be parsed and can wander. For years, teams trained small classifiers for each such question, which are fast but rigid: every new question needed new labelled data.

Decision models try to combine the two. You pass the input and a typed question: a yes or no question, a choice among options, or a score. The model answers in one forward pass, producing probabilities rather than prose.

The label comes from the math, not from generating text, so latency is a few milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, the answer type is guaranteed, and the confidence can be used to decide what to do next.

The framing comes from Kahneman's System One and System Two. System One is quick intuition. System Two is slow reasoning. In the architecture proposed, a System One decision model handles the high-volume routine calls and passes the uncertain ones up to a reasoning model.

Vendors in this area, from late 2026, include Jev from TypeSafe, the open Laya built on ModernBERT, and Clef, built on a Qwen language model by a large infrastructure provider. These are weeks old; treat their reported figures as marketing until you test them on your data.

The course has four parts. First the building blocks: encoder models such as ModernBERT, and how a generalised classifier works. Then the typed-question interface and two architectures, a masked-token encoder design and a prefill-only decoder design.

Then calibration, evaluation and how to build your own test. Last, putting decision models into systems with routing, thresholds, guardrails and cost maths. Each chapter has labs in plain Python that implement the key calculations.

practice.title: Match the term
practice.intro: Pair each idea with its meaning.

practice.title: Softmax to answer
practice.intro: Write decide(options, logits): softmax the logits and return [best option, its probability rounded to 3 decimals] (first option on ties).
practice.solution:
import math
def decide(options, logits):
    m = max(logits)
    e = [math.exp(v - m) for v in logits]
    t = sum(e)
    p = [v / t for v in e]
    b = 0
    for i in range(len(p)):
        if p[i] > p[b] + 1e-12:
            b = i
    return [options[b], round(p[b], 3)]

practice.title: Escalate or answer
practice.intro: Write route(probs, threshold): return 'answer' if the largest probability is at least threshold, else 'escalate'.
practice.solution:
def route(probs, threshold):
    return 'answer' if max(probs) >= threshold else 'escalate'

practice.title: Share handled cheaply
practice.intro: Write handled_share(confidences, threshold): the fraction of confidences at or above threshold, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: How many stay on the fast path?

practice.title: Expected cost
practice.intro: Write expected_cost(share_fast, cost_fast, cost_slow): the average cost per request when share_fast of requests cost cost_fast and the rest, plus the fast attempt, cost cost_slow in addition (every request first pays cost_fast). Round to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Everyone pays for the fast model.
practice.solution:
def expected_cost(share_fast, cost_fast, cost_slow):
    return round(cost_fast + (1 - share_fast) * cost_slow, 4)

practice.intro: Write answer_or_none(options, probs, threshold): the option with the highest probability if that probability is at least threshold, else None.

chapters.title: Encoders and generalised classifiers: from BERT to ModernBERT

maps.title: Encoders
links: Encoder | reads | Whole text both ways
Classification head | maps | Vector to label

summary: Encoders turn text into contextual vectors. A small head on top turns a vector into a label. Fine-tuned on a few thousand examples, this is the classic classifier and still the efficient choice for many tasks.

Generalised classifiers avoid retraining per label set: zero-shot natural language inference frames each label as a hypothesis to test, embedding models match text to label descriptions, and cross-encoders score a text and a candidate together.

ModernBERT, released at the end of 2024, updates the BERT encoder with rotary positions, alternating local and global attention, unpadding, FlashAttention and an eight-thousand-token context. It is the base on which Laya is reported to be built.

glossary.def: A transformer that reads the whole input with attention in both directions and outputs a vector for every token.
A small layer on top of an encoder that maps a vector to label scores.
Choosing among labels never seen in training, usually by testing each label as an entailment hypothesis.
A model that reads a text and a candidate together and outputs a relevance or match score.
A 2024 update of BERT with longer context and faster, more modern components.

keyPoints: NLI zero-shot: premise = text, hypothesis = 'This is about X'.
Bi-encoder is fast, cross-encoder is accurate.
Fine-tuning needs hundreds to thousands of labels.

items: ELI5. Teach a helper to read a whole sentence and pick a sticker for it. That is a classifier. The reading part is called an encoder.
An encoder reads all of a text at once. Every token can attend to every other, left and right, so the vector for each token is informed by the whole sentence.

Put a head on the vector for the first token or on the average of all tokens, a linear layer producing one score per label, and train on labelled examples with cross-entropy loss. That is a fine-tuned classifier.
At a few hundred million parameters it runs in milliseconds on a modest GPU or a CPU, and for fixed label sets it remains hard to beat on cost.

Its weakness is the fixed label set. Generalised classifiers address that. The zero-shot trick uses a model trained on natural language inference, which decides whether a premise entails a hypothesis.
To classify 'My card was charged twice' you ask, for each candidate label, whether the text entails 'This message is about billing', 'about shipping' and so on, and compare the entailment scores.
An embedding model offers another route: encode the text and the label descriptions separately and pick the nearest. A cross-encoder reads text and label together, slower but sharper.

lesson.code:
from transformers import pipeline
clf = pipeline('zero-shot-classification', model='facebook/bart-large-mnli')
out = clf('My card was charged twice',
          candidate_labels=['billing', 'shipping', 'account'])
print(out['labels'], out['scores'])

items: BERT dates from 2018, and the field learned much since. ModernBERT, published by Answer.AI and LightOn at the end of 2024, brings the encoder up to date: rotary position embeddings, alternating local and global attention layers for efficiency, removal of padding tokens, FlashAttention kernels, a vocabulary trained on code as well as text, and a context of 8,192 tokens instead of 512.
It comes in a base size near 150 million parameters and a large size near 400 million. It is faster than older encoders, and its long context matters for classifying documents.

Why does this matter for decision models? A decision model needs to read an input, understand a question and options, and produce calibrated scores. An encoder reads everything both ways in one pass and is small, so it is a natural base.
The next chapters show how option markers and typed heads turn an encoder into a general decision maker, and how the same idea carries over to decoder models.

chapters.title: The typed-question interface

maps.title: Typed questions
links: Yes or no | gives | One probability

summary: A decision model is queried with a structured request: the input, a context or state, optional criteria, and a typed question. The type fixes the output: a probability for yes or no, a distribution over options for a choice, or a bounded score.
Because the answer comes from a head rather than generated text, it is always well formed. The caller sets the policy: thresholds, how to treat low confidence and when to escalate.
Good questions are specific, mutually exclusive and checkable. Designing the question and options is the main job of the person using a decision model.

glossary.def: A request whose answer type is fixed in advance: boolean, one of several options, or a numeric score.
A short statement of the rules or standards the decision should follow.
Extra context passed with the input, such as user history or the current step of a workflow.
The list of allowed answers for a choice question.
Declining to answer, or flagging low confidence, instead of forcing a choice.

keyPoints: Score: a value in a range, such as 0 to 1.
Put hard rules in criteria, not in hope.

items: ELI5. Instead of letting the helper talk, ask a multiple choice question: yes or no, A B or C, or a number from zero to ten. The answer is always tidy.

Think of a decision model as a function with a strict signature. You give it an input, perhaps a state, perhaps criteria, and a question. Vendors differ in names. A reported API from this field uses three question types: a yes or no kind, a choice among options, and a score.
Whatever the names, the pattern is the same, and it is worth learning because it determines what you can build.
A boolean question yields one probability that the answer is yes. Is this email a phishing attempt? Does this reply violate the refund policy?

A choice question yields a distribution over listed options that sums to one: which department should handle this ticket? A score question yields a number in a range: how urgent is this, from zero to one? All three produce numbers, not prose, so your code can compare them with thresholds, log them, and plot them.

lesson.code:
# a typed request, as plain data
request = {
    'input': 'The customer says the parcel never arrived and wants money back.',
    'state': {'order_age_days': 12, 'tier': 'gold'},
    'criteria': 'Refunds over 100 dollars need a human.',
    'question': {'type': 'choice',
                 'options': ['refund', 'reship', 'escalate', 'reply']},
}
valid = request['question']['type'] in ('boolean', 'choice', 'score')

items: Question design matters more than people expect. Options should be mutually exclusive and cover the cases, with an 'other' or 'escalate' option for the rest. Criteria should state rules plainly. State, such as order age or earlier steps, lets the model use context it cannot see in the text.
Ask one thing at a time: 'Is this urgent and about billing?' is two questions. A score needs an anchored scale, so say what 0 and 1 mean.

Then you decide what to do with the answer, and that policy belongs to you, not to the model. Typical policies: act automatically above a high threshold, escalate in a grey zone, and reject or defer below.

Different mistakes cost different amounts, so thresholds should be set from your own data, as a later chapter shows. Keep a log of questions, probabilities and outcomes; it is your evaluation set for tomorrow.

chapters.title: Masked-option encoder designs (the Laya pattern)

maps.title: Laya pattern
links: Option marker | is | A mask slot

summary: One design for a decision model puts the input and the options into a single encoder prompt, each option followed by a mask token. After one pass, the vector at each mask is scored by a small head, and a softmax across the masks gives the option probabilities.
Laya is reported to follow this pattern on a ModernBERT base of about 421 million parameters, offered openly. Details come from vendor material and may change; the pattern is what matters.
Such a design is fast and small but limited by the encoder's context, its pretraining and the amount of adaptation. Specialised domains usually need fine-tuning.

glossary.def: A mask token placed after each candidate option so the encoder produces one vector per option.
Reading the input and all options together so each option's vector is informed by the others.
A small layer that turns each option vector into a score.
Dividing logits by a constant before softmax to soften or sharpen probabilities.
Further training on your own labelled decisions.

items: ELI5. Show the helper the story and the choices together, with a blank after each choice. Each blank gets a score, and the biggest score wins.

Here is one way to build a decision model out of an encoder, described in material about Laya, an open decision model reported to be based on ModernBERT. Write the input, then each option, and after each option put a special mask token. Feed the whole string to the encoder.

Because attention runs both ways, the vector at each mask token has seen the input and all the other options. A tiny head scores each of those vectors, and a softmax across the options gives probabilities.

lesson.code:
# the idea, in pseudocode
text = 'Customer: my card was charged twice'
options = ['billing', 'shipping', 'account']
prompt = text + ' [SEP] ' + ' '.join(o + ' [MASK]' for o in options)
hidden = encoder(prompt)                 # one forward pass
scores = [head(hidden[i]) for i in mask_positions]
probs = softmax([s / temperature for s in scores])

items: The attractions are plain. It is one forward pass over a few hundred tokens, so on suitable hardware it takes milliseconds. The model is small enough to run on your own machine, which helps with privacy and cost.

The options are inputs, not fixed outputs, so you can change them per request without retraining. The training task, predicting which option is right, matches pretraining on masked tokens, so the encoder transfers well.

The limits are also plain. The encoder's context bounds the length of input plus options, so the 8,192 tokens of ModernBERT are a ceiling. Tasks needing multi-step reasoning, arithmetic, or deep world knowledge are not a good fit; the model is deciding, not thinking.

Off-the-shelf quality on your domain is unknown until measured, and the reports say that fine-tuning on a few hundred or thousand of your own labelled examples is often what makes it strong. The reported figures from the vendors should be re-tested.

Temperature deserves a note. Raw softmax outputs from a neural network are often overconfident. A single number, the temperature, divides the logits before the softmax. Above one it flattens probabilities, below one it sharpens them. You choose it on held-out data to make confidence match accuracy.
The calibration chapter makes this precise. Meanwhile, remember that a decision model's probabilities are only useful if they are trustworthy.

def build_prompt(text, options):

practice.title: Mask positions
practice.intro: Write mask_positions(tokens): the indexes where the token is '[MASK]'.
practice.solution:
def mask_positions(tokens):
    return [i for i in range(len(tokens)) if tokens[i] == '[MASK]']

practice.title: Temperature softmax
practice.intro: Write probs(scores, T): softmax of scores / T rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def probs(scores, T):
    s = [v / T for v in scores]
    m = max(s)
    e = [math.exp(v - m) for v in s]
    t = sum(e)
    return [round(v / t, 4) for v in e]

chapters.title: Decoder-based decision models (the Clef pattern)

maps.title: Clef pattern
links: Pointer head | picks | An input span

summary: The other route builds a decision model on a decoder language model but never generates text. It runs only the prefill pass over the prompt, then reads the final hidden state with small heads.
That keeps the language model's knowledge and instruction following while skipping slow token-by-token generation.

Clef, from Cloudflare, is reported to use Qwen-based models of roughly 9 and 27 billion parameters with a joint schema head that fills several typed answers at once, and a pointer head that selects a span or item from the input. A related Kev design is described as a pointer head.
Reported benefits are speed, typed outputs and shared computation through KV-cache reuse. Reports differ between sources, so verify specifics before relying on them.

glossary.def: The phase where a decoder processes the whole prompt in parallel before generating; a decision model stops here.
Stored attention keys and values from earlier tokens, reusable when the prompt shares a prefix.
A head that outputs several typed fields, such as a boolean, a choice and a score, from one pass.
A head that picks a position or item in the input rather than a label from a fixed set.
Handling more than text, for example images with text.

keyPoints: Shared prefix: reuse the KV cache.

items: ELI5. A bigger helper reads the whole question but stops before writing an answer. That is fast, because writing is the slow part.

A decoder language model like Llama or Qwen is built to generate: read the prompt, then emit one token at a time. The prompt phase, prefill, is a single parallel pass and is cheap per token. The generation phase is sequential and dominates latency, since each new token needs another pass.
If you only need a decision, not an essay, you can stop after prefill, read the last hidden state, and feed it to a small head. That turns a language model into a decision model.
What do you gain over an encoder? A decoder with billions of parameters has more world knowledge, follows instructions and handles long, messy prompts, and can accept images if it is multimodal.
What do you lose? It is bigger and slower than a 400-million-parameter encoder, though still far faster than a model that writes a chain of thought.
Clef, announced by Cloudflare in 2026 and built on Qwen models reported at about 27 and 9 billion parameters, is the first well-known example of this pattern.

lesson.code:
# prefill-only decision, in pseudocode
hidden = decoder.prefill(prompt)[-1]        # last token state, no generation
schema = {'urgent': 'boolean',
          'team': ['billing', 'tech', 'sales'],
          'priority': 'score'}
out = {name: head[name](hidden) for name in schema}
# one pass fills every field; none can be malformed

items: Two head ideas recur. A joint schema head answers several typed questions in one pass, so one prefill yields a boolean, a choice and a score together.

A pointer head selects an item from the input itself, for example which of twenty tool descriptions or which retrieved passage best fits, which suits agent routing where the options are long and different each time. Both guarantee well-formed answers, unlike parsing generated text.

Because many requests share a long prefix, such as the same instructions, tool list or document, serving systems keep the attention keys and values of the shared part in a KV cache, so only the new suffix needs computing.

For decision models that ask many questions about the same document this can make a large difference. You can run such models yourself: open weights and runtimes such as Unsloth and Ollama-style servers are mentioned in the project documentation.
Remember the caveat that this category is only weeks old, and sources disagree on details.

chapters.title: Calibration: making probabilities trustworthy
summary: A decision model is only useful if its probabilities mean something: of the cases where it says 90 percent, about 90 percent should be right. Neural networks are often overconfident, so we measure and repair calibration.

Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy. Brier score and log loss are proper scoring rules that reward honest probabilities. Temperature scaling fixes much overconfidence with a single parameter fitted on held-out data.
Some vendors train for calibration directly, with reinforcement learning on calibration objectives; reports describe this as a selling point, which you should test yourself.

glossary.def: The match between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies.
The weighted average gap between confidence and accuracy across confidence bins.
The mean squared difference between predicted probability and the 0 or 1 outcome.
The mean negative log probability assigned to the true outcome.
Dividing logits by a fitted constant to repair over- or under-confidence.

keyPoints: ECE = sum over bins of (n_bin / n) |acc - conf|.
Fit T on a validation set, not the test set.

items: ELI5. If a helper says 'I am 90 percent sure' ten times, nine should be right. If only five are, it is bragging.

Suppose a model says 'refund approved, 95 percent' a thousand times. If 95 percent of those were correct, it is calibrated at that level. If only 80 percent were, it is overconfident, and a threshold of 0.9 will let through many mistakes.
Modern networks tend to be overconfident because they are trained to push the loss down on the training data, which rewards ever larger logits.

To measure calibration, sort predictions into bins by confidence, say 0.5 to 0.6, 0.6 to 0.7 and so on. In each bin compare the average confidence with the fraction correct. Plotting accuracy against confidence gives a reliability diagram: a perfect model lies on the diagonal.

Expected calibration error is the average of the gaps, weighted by bin size. Two scoring rules summarise both sharpness and calibration. The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probability. Log loss is the mean negative log probability of the truth, and punishes confident mistakes harshly.
The repair that works surprisingly often is temperature scaling. Keep the model fixed, hold out a validation set, and find the single number T that minimises log loss when logits are divided by T.

When the model is overconfident T comes out above one, which flattens the probabilities without changing which option is top. Accuracy stays the same; only confidence changes. For richer problems there are other methods, such as isotonic regression, but start simple.
Some decision-model vendors describe training with a calibration-aware reinforcement objective, reported under the name RLCD, to make confidence honest from the start.
Whether that works for your data is an empirical question, and the answer depends on the shift between their training data and your inputs.
Always check calibration on your own held-out cases, re-check after fine-tuning or changing the question wording, and monitor it in production, because the world changes.

practice.intro: A model's confidences and outcomes are plotted as a reliability diagram. Drag the temperature slider to repair the overconfident model and watch ECE fall. Reach an ECE below 0.04 to complete the lab.

practice.title: Match the metric
practice.intro: Pair each metric with its idea.

practice.title: Brier score
practice.intro: Write brier(probs, outcomes): the mean of (p - y)^2 where outcomes are 0 or 1; rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
def brier(probs, outcomes):
    return round(sum([(p - y) ** 2 for p, y in zip(probs, outcomes)]) / len(probs), 4)

practice.title: Log loss
practice.intro: Write log_loss(probs, outcomes): the mean of -log(p) when the outcome is 1 and -log(1-p) when it is 0; rounded to 4 decimals.

practice.title: Expected calibration error
practice.intro: Write ece(conf, correct, bins): split [0, 1] into equal bins (a value belongs to bin min(int(c * bins), bins - 1)); the sum over non-empty bins of (n_bin / n) |mean(correct) - mean(conf)|, rounded to 4 decimals.

practice.title: Reliability bins
practice.intro: Write reliability(conf, correct, bins): for each non-empty bin (bin of c is min(int(c * bins), bins - 1)) return [bin index, count, mean confidence, accuracy], with the last two rounded to 3 decimals.

practice.title: Apply temperature to a pair
practice.intro: Write calibrate(logit, T): the sigmoid of logit / T rounded to 4 decimals.

practice.title: Best temperature
practice.intro: Write fit_temperature(logits, outcomes, candidates): the candidate T with the lowest log loss of sigmoid(logit / T) against 0 or 1 outcomes (first on ties).
practice.solution:
import math
def fit_temperature(logits, outcomes, candidates):
    best = None
    bl = None
    for T in candidates:
        loss = 0.0
        for z, y in zip(logits, outcomes):
            p = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z / T))
            loss = loss - math.log(p if y == 1 else 1 - p)
        loss = round(loss, 9)
        if bl is None or loss < bl:
            bl = loss
            best = T
    return best

practice.title: Threshold for target precision
practice.intro: Write threshold_for_precision(conf, correct, target): the smallest confidence value present in conf such that the precision of all predictions with confidence at or above it is at least target; return None if none.

chapters.title: Evaluating decision models
summary: Do not rely on a vendor's headline numbers. Reports in this field include a Decision Index and results on public tasks such as BANKING77 intent classification, but they are self-reported and may not match your data.

Build a labelled test set from your own traffic, measure accuracy, calibration, per-class errors, cost-weighted loss and latency at your batch size, and compare against a simple baseline and against a large LLM.
Check the effect of fine-tuning: a few hundred of your own examples often add the most. Keep a separate untouched test set and watch for leakage.

glossary.def: Labelled examples held out from all training and tuning, used to estimate real performance.
A table giving the cost of each kind of mistake, used to choose thresholds.
A simple reference such as the majority class or keyword rules, to show the added value.
Test data leaking into training, which inflates scores.
A reported composite benchmark for decision models; treat as a vendor measure until independently checked.

keyPoints: Report accuracy, calibration, latency and cost.
Compare with a baseline and with an LLM.

items: ELI5. Before trusting a new helper, give them your own quiz, not theirs. Count mistakes, and which mistakes cost more.

When a new model claims to beat everything, your first move is not to read the leaderboard but to build a test. Collect a few hundred real inputs, label them carefully (ideally by two people so you measure disagreement), and set them aside.
This is the only number that predicts how the system will behave for you.

Public results are context. For the decision models in this chapter's sources, vendors report scores on a composite they call the Decision Index and on well-known tasks like BANKING77, a set of seventy-seven banking intents.

Such numbers come with the usual caveats: they are self-reported, the prompts and options may be favourable, training data may overlap with test data, and the field changes monthly, with different articles giving different figures. Quote them as 'reported by the vendor, as of date' and verify.

lesson.code:
from collections import Counter
def report(y_true, y_pred):
    acc = sum(a == b for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)
    errors = Counter((a, b) for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred) if a != b)
    return acc, errors.most_common(5)   # which confusions matter most

items: Accuracy is not enough. Look at per-class precision and recall, since rare but costly classes can hide behind a good average. Use a cost matrix: wrongly auto-approving a fraud costs far more than sending a good case to review.
Check calibration, as in the last chapter, and measure latency and throughput on your own hardware with your own batch size, since a vendor's milliseconds assume their setup.
Finally compare options fairly. A keyword baseline tells you what the model adds. A large LLM given the same question is the quality ceiling and the cost reference.

Fine-tune the decision model on part of your data to see headroom; if a few hundred examples lift accuracy a lot, the base model was not enough alone. Re-run the test whenever the model, the options wording or the input mix changes, and keep sampling live traffic for new labels.

practice.title: Accuracy
practice.intro: Write accuracy(y_true, y_pred): the fraction correct, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.solution:
def accuracy(y_true, y_pred):
    return round(sum([1 for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred) if a == b]) / float(len(y_true)), 3)

practice.title: Per-class precision and recall
practice.intro: Write prf(y_true, y_pred, label): [precision, recall] for the label, each rounded to 3 decimals (0 when undefined).
practice.solution:
def prf(y_true, y_pred, label):
    tp = len([1 for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred) if a == label and b == label])
    pp = len([b for b in y_pred if b == label])
    ap = len([a for a in y_true if a == label])
    p = tp / float(pp) if pp else 0
    r = tp / float(ap) if ap else 0
    return [round(p, 3), round(r, 3)]

practice.title: Confusion pairs
practice.intro: Write confusions(y_true, y_pred): [true, predicted, count] triples for every wrong prediction, sorted by count descending then alphabetically.

practice.title: Cost-weighted error
practice.intro: Write total_cost(y_true, y_pred, cost): cost is a list of [true, predicted, price] triples; wrong predictions not listed cost 1; correct ones cost 0. Return the total.

practice.title: Best threshold by cost
practice.intro: Write best_threshold(conf, correct, candidates, c_wrong, c_review): for each candidate t, answered cases (conf >= t) cost c_wrong if wrong; the rest cost c_review each. Return the candidate with the lowest total cost (first on ties).
practice.hint: Trade review cost against error cost.

practice.title: Percentile latency
practice.intro: Write percentile(values, q): the nearest-rank percentile: sort values and return the element at rank ceil(q / 100 x n) (1-based).
practice.hint: Tail latency matters more than the mean.
practice.solution:
import math
def percentile(values, q):
    s = sorted(values)
    k = int(math.ceil(q / 100.0 * len(s)))
    return s[max(k, 1) - 1]

chapters.title: Decision models in real systems

maps.title: Systems
links: Escalation | calls | Big model or human

summary: The usual home for a decision model is a cascade: the fast model decides most cases, the uncertain ones escalate to a large LLM or a human, and the outcomes feed back into the evaluation data. Cost and latency fall while quality is kept by the thresholds.

Typical uses are routing support tickets and agent tool calls, content and policy guardrails, verifying that an answer matches its sources, relevance filtering, and workflow gates. Open models can be run locally for privacy.
Plan for failure: distribution shift, adversarial inputs, over-trust in confidence and silent changes in vendor models. Humans stay responsible for high-stakes decisions.

glossary.def: A chain of models from cheap and fast to expensive and accurate, with each stage answering only when confident.
A check placed before or after a model to enforce policy, safety or format.
A component that sends each request to the best model or tool.
A change in the inputs over time, so past accuracy no longer holds.
A person reviews or decides cases the system is unsure about or that carry high risk.

keyPoints: Fast model first, escalate when unsure.

items: ELI5. Put the quick helper at the door. When it is unsure it calls the expert or a person, and keeps a diary so it can learn.

Put the pieces together. A request arrives. A decision model reads it and answers the typed question in a few milliseconds. If its confidence clears the threshold, the system acts. If not, it escalates: to a large reasoning model that thinks step by step, or to a person.

Suppose eighty percent of traffic clears the bar. Then the expensive path serves a fifth of requests, and average cost and latency drop several-fold, while accuracy on the escalated cases comes from the strong model.

Decision models fit several jobs. Routing: which team, which tool, which model. Guardrails: is this input safe, is this output on topic, does it follow the policy. Verification: does the answer follow from the retrieved sources. Gating in agents: should the agent continue, ask the user, or stop.
Filtering: which of a hundred retrieved passages is relevant, using a pointer head. In all of them the decision is small and frequent, which is where a fast model beats a big one.

Where it runs matters. Open weights can be served on your own hardware with common tools, which keeps sensitive text in your own network and removes per-call fees, at the price of operating the system yourself. Hosted APIs are easier to start with but send data out and can change under you.
Pin the model version, and re-run your evaluation when it updates.

Plan for failure. Inputs drift, so watch accuracy and calibration on a sample of live traffic. Adversarial users will write inputs that fool a classifier, so guardrails need layers and monitoring. Confidence can be misleading outside the training distribution.

Keep a human path for high-stakes cases, record why decisions were made, and be open with users about automation. This is a young technology: use it where mistakes are cheap and reversible first, measure, and expand carefully.

practice.title: Guardrail check
practice.intro: Write allowed(label, p, blocked, threshold): False if label is in the blocked list and p is at least threshold, else True.
practice.solution:
def allowed(label, p, blocked, threshold):
    return not (label in blocked and p >= threshold)

practice.title: Drift check
practice.intro: Write drifted(old_acc, new_acc, tolerance): True if new_acc is lower than old_acc by more than tolerance.
practice.solution:
def drifted(old_acc, new_acc, tolerance):
    return (old_acc - new_acc) > tolerance + 1e-12

practice.title: Break-even share
practice.intro: Write break_even(small_cost, big_cost): the minimum share of requests the small model must handle alone for a cascade to cost no more than always calling the big model; share = small_cost / big_cost, rounded to 4 decimals, capped at 1.
practice.hint: Everyone pays for the small model, so the savings must exceed it.
practice.solution:
def break_even(small_cost, big_cost):
    return round(min(1.0, small_cost / float(big_cost)), 4)
